title: Equations
outcomes: Tell a conditional equation from an identity and classify equations by degree (linear, quadratic, cubic).
Solve linear equations in one unknown, and simultaneous linear equations in two and three unknowns by elimination, substitution and cross-multiplication.
Solve quadratic equations, use the sum and product of roots, form an equation from given roots and judge the nature of roots from the discriminant.
Solve equations reducible to quadratics and cubic equations (trial root and factorisation), and translate business word problems into equations.

meta.exam_tip: In the exam most equation MCQs are fastest by substituting the four options back into the equation. Learn −b/a, c/a and the discriminant cold — they answer many questions without solving anything.

concepts.title: What an equation is — conditional equation vs identity
body: An equation is a statement that two expressions are equal. If the equality holds only for some values of the variable, it is a conditional equation; if it holds for every value, it is an identity.
A value of the variable that makes the equation true is a root (solution). Finding all roots is solving the equation.
The degree of an equation is the highest power of the unknown after simplification: degree 1 — linear (simple); degree 2 — quadratic; degree 3 — cubic. An equation of degree n has at most n roots.
Two or more linear equations that must be satisfied together by the same values are called simultaneous linear equations.
concepts.analogy: An identity is like "a dozen = 12" — always true. A conditional equation is a lock that opens only for the right combination.
concepts.work: Every pricing, break-even or allocation question a client asks ("at what volume do we stop losing money?") is first written as an equation and then solved.

concepts.title: Linear (simple) equations in one unknown
body: Standard form: ax + b = 0 with a ≠ 0; the single root is x = −b/a.
Method: clear fractions by multiplying by the LCM of the denominators, collect terms in x on one side and constants on the other (transposition changes the sign), then divide by the coefficient of x.

Word problems: name the unknown clearly ("let the son’s present age be x years"), translate each sentence into algebra, solve, and check the answer against the original words — not just against your equation.
concepts.analogy: Solving is like balancing a weighing scale: whatever you do to one pan you must do to the other.
concepts.work: Break-even volume = fixed cost ÷ (selling price − variable cost per unit) is just the solution of a linear equation in the number of units.

concepts.title: Simultaneous linear equations in two unknowns
body: Elimination: multiply the equations by suitable numbers so that one unknown has the same coefficient, then add or subtract to remove it. Substitution: express one unknown from one equation and put it into the other.
Cross-multiplication: for a₁x + b₁y + c₁ = 0 and a₂x + b₂y + c₂ = 0, x/(b₁c₂ − b₂c₁) = y/(c₁a₂ − c₂a₁) = 1/(a₁b₂ − a₂b₁). Keep every equation in the "= 0" form with signs, or the answer flips.

Number of solutions: if a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂ the lines intersect — a unique solution. If a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂ the lines are parallel — no solution (inconsistent). If all three ratios are equal the lines coincide — infinitely many solutions.
concepts.analogy: Two equations are two clues in a detective story; each one alone leaves many suspects, together they point to one.
concepts.work: Product-mix questions — how many units of two products use up the machine hours and labour hours exactly — are pairs of simultaneous equations.

concepts.title: Three linear equations in three unknowns
body: Pick one unknown and eliminate it from two different pairs of equations. This leaves two equations in two unknowns; solve them, then back-substitute to find the third.
Shortcut patterns: when the equations are x + y, y + z, z + x type, add all three to get x + y + z first.
Always substitute the answer into the equation you did not use for elimination — it is the quickest check.
concepts.analogy: Like peeling an onion: remove one layer (one unknown) at a time until a single value is left.
concepts.work: Allocating joint costs or service-department costs among three departments leads to three equations in three unknowns (the "simultaneous equation method" in cost accounting).

concepts.title: Quadratic equations — solving, sum and product of roots
body: Standard form ax² + bx + c = 0, a ≠ 0. Solve by factorisation (split the middle term so that the two parts multiply to ac) or by the formula x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)] / 2a.
If α and β are the roots: α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a.
An equation with roots α and β is x² − (sum of roots)x + (product of roots) = 0.
Useful identities: α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ; (α − β)² = (α + β)² − 4αβ; 1/α + 1/β = (α + β)/αβ; α³ + β³ = (α + β)³ − 3αβ(α + β).
concepts.analogy: −b/a and c/a are the "fingerprints" of a quadratic: you can identify the pair of roots without ever meeting them.
concepts.work: Revenue that depends on price (price × demand) gives a quadratic profit function; its roots are the break-even prices.

concepts.title: Nature of roots — the discriminant
body: The discriminant is D = b² − 4ac. For an equation with rational coefficients: D = 0 → roots real and equal; D > 0 and a perfect square → real, rational and unequal; D > 0 but not a perfect square → real, irrational and unequal; D < 0 → imaginary (no real roots).
Irrational roots come in conjugate pairs: if p + √q is a root, so is p − √q. Imaginary roots also come in conjugate pairs.
Special cases: roots reciprocal of each other → product 1, so c = a. Roots equal in magnitude and opposite in sign → sum 0, so b = 0. One root zero → c = 0.
concepts.analogy: The discriminant is a weather forecast for the roots: zero — one clear answer; positive — two answers; negative — no real answer at all.
concepts.work: Before spending time solving, a quick D-check tells you whether a pricing or rate equation even has a real answer.

concepts.title: Equations reducible to quadratics and word problems
body: Substitution turns many equations into quadratics: x⁴ − 13x² + 36 = 0 (put y = x²); x − 5√x + 6 = 0 (put y = √x); x + 1/x = k (multiply through by x); expressions repeated in brackets (put y = the bracket).
After substituting back, reject values that are impossible — a square root cannot be negative, a count of people cannot be fractional, a price cannot be negative.
Typical word problems: numbers and their reciprocals, consecutive integers, digits of a number, sharing a fixed cost among people, cost price and quantity, speed and time.
concepts.analogy: A disguised quadratic is a quadratic wearing a costume — substitution removes the costume.
concepts.work: Cost-sharing and "if the price were lower we could buy more" situations are everyday versions of these problems in procurement and budgeting.

concepts.title: Cubic equations
body: A cubic ax³ + bx² + cx + d = 0 has at most three roots. In this paper the cubic usually has an integer root that you find by trial (try ±1, ±2, ±3 — divisors of the constant term).
If x = k makes the expression zero, then (x − k) is a factor (factor theorem). Divide to get a quadratic and solve it.
Root relations: α + β + γ = −b/a; αβ + βγ + γα = c/a; αβγ = −d/a. These check an answer quickly or use extra information such as "the product of two roots is 12".
In MCQs, simply substitute the given triplets — any option with a value that fails is eliminated.
concepts.analogy: Finding one root of a cubic is like finding the first loose thread; pull it and the rest unravels into a quadratic.
concepts.work: Cubics appear in volume-based packaging costs and in some multi-period rate calculations; in practice spreadsheets solve them, but the trial-root idea is the same.

solution.text: LCM of 4, 3 and 2 is 12. Multiply every term by 12: 3(x + 3) − 4(x − 2) = 6.
Check: 14/4 − 9/3 = 3.5 − 3 = 0.5. ✔ Watch the sign when removing −4(x − 2): it gives +8.

illustrations.title: Age problem
illustrations.q: A father is four times as old as his son. After five years he will be three times as old as his son. Find their present ages.

solution.text: Let the son’s present age be S years; the father’s is 4S.
Son 10 years, father 40 years. Check: after 5 years, 45 = 3 × 15. ✔

illustrations.title: Two equations — elimination and cross-multiplication
illustrations.q: Solve 3x + 4y = 18 and 5x − 2y = 4 (a) by elimination, (b) by cross-multiplication.

solution.text: (a) Multiply the second equation by 2: 10x − 4y = 8. Add to the first: 13x = 26 → x = 2. Then 4y = 18 − 6 → y = 3.
(b) Write both in "= 0" form: 3x + 4y − 18 = 0 and 5x − 2y − 4 = 0, so a₁ = 3, b₁ = 4, c₁ = −18, a₂ = 5, b₂ = −2, c₂ = −4.

illustrations.title: Quadratic by formula; sum and product of roots
illustrations.q: Solve 6x² − 7x − 20 = 0 and verify the sum and product of the roots.

illustrations.title: Nature of roots and forming new equations
illustrations.q: (a) Find k if 4x² − kx + 9 = 0 has equal roots. (b) If α, β are the roots of x² − 5x + 3 = 0, form the equation whose roots are α² and β². (c) Form the quadratic with rational coefficients one of whose roots is 3 + √2.

solution.text: (b) α + β = 5, αβ = 3. Sum of new roots α² + β² = 25 − 6 = 19; product α²β² = 9. Equation: x² − 19x + 9 = 0.
(c) Irrational roots come in conjugate pairs, so the other root is 3 − √2. Sum = 6, product = 9 − 2 = 7. Equation: x² − 6x + 7 = 0.

checks.label: k for equal roots of 4x² − kx + 9 = 0 (positive value)

illustrations.title: Disguised quadratic and a purchase problem
illustrations.q: (a) Solve x⁴ − 13x² + 36 = 0. (b) A shop spends ₹600 on pens. If each pen cost ₹5 less, it could buy 4 more pens for the same money. Find the price of a pen.

solution.text: D = 25 + 3,000 = 3025 = 55². p = (5 + 55)/2 = 30 (the negative root −25 is rejected).

checks.label: check: 4 more pens at the lower price

solution.text: Try x = 1: 1 − 7 + 6 = 0, so (x − 1) is a factor.
Roots: 1, 2, −3. Check: sum = 0 = −b/a (there is no x² term). ✔

checks.label: f(1) = 0, so x − 1 is a factor

jobs.title: Break-even volume for a new product
jobs.role: Management accountant in an FMCG company
jobs.situation: Fixed costs of a new line are ₹3,60,000 a month. Each unit sells for ₹250 and costs ₹160 in variable cost. The CFO asks how many units must be sold to break even.
steps: Let the number of units be x. Revenue = 250x; total cost = 3,60,000 + 160x.
Present it with the contribution per unit (₹90) so the CFO sees how sensitive the answer is to price.
jobs.takeaway: Break-even is a linear equation; the contribution per unit is the coefficient of x.
jobs.think: If the price falls to ₹240, what happens to break-even volume?
jobs.answer: Contribution falls to ₹80, so break-even rises to 3,60,000 ÷ 80 = 4,500 units.

jobs.title: Using up machine and labour hours exactly
jobs.situation: Product A needs 2 machine hours and 3 labour hours; product B needs 4 machine hours and 1 labour hour. Next month 2,000 machine hours and 1,500 labour hours are available and management wants both fully used.
steps: From the second, b = 1,500 − 3a. Substitute: 2a + 6,000 − 12a = 2,000 → a = 400.
jobs.takeaway: Simultaneous equations answer "how much of each" when every resource must be fully used.
jobs.think: Is full use of both resources always the most profitable plan?
jobs.answer: Not necessarily — profit depends on contribution per unit. Choosing the best plan under limits is the linear-inequalities topic of the next chapter.

jobs.title: Back-solving the rate on a deposit
jobs.situation: A client’s two-year bank deposit of ₹5,00,000 matured at ₹5,83,200 with annual compounding. You need the rate to check against the bank’s certificate.
steps: Take the square root: 1 + r = 1.08 (the negative root −1.08 is meaningless for a rate).
Match it with the certificate; any gap is a query for the client.
jobs.takeaway: A pure quadratic (no x term) is solved by taking the square root — then discard the root that makes no business sense.
jobs.answer: It would give r = −208%, which is impossible for a deposit that grew in value.

questions.q: Solve: 2x + y − z = 3; x + 2y + z = 9; 3x − y + 2z = 10. Show the elimination steps.

scheme.pt: Eliminates the same variable from two pairs

remarks: Most errors come from eliminating different variables from the two pairs, which leaves three unknowns again.
mistakes: Back-substituting into the wrong equation and not checking.
tips: Number your equations and say which ones you combine.
In the MCQ version, just substitute the four option-triplets.

questions.q: A group of friends hires a bus for ₹14,400, sharing the cost equally. Four friends drop out, and each of the rest pays ₹600 more. How many friends were there originally?

model.text: Let the original number be n. Original share = 14,400/n; new share = 14,400/(n − 4).

scheme.pt: n = 12; rejects negative root with reason

remarks: Candidates who subtract the shares the wrong way round get n² − 4n + 96 = 0, which has no real roots — a signal that the set-up is wrong. Those who write n + 4 instead of n − 4 get n² + 4n − 96 = 0 and the wrong answer 8 — always check against the story.
mistakes: Subtracting in the wrong order (old share − new share).
tips: Write "let n = …" with units; it earns the set-up mark.

questions.q: Solve x³ − 4x² + x + 6 = 0 and verify your roots using the sum and product relations.

model.text: Try divisors of 6. x = −1: −1 − 4 − 1 + 6 = 0, so (x + 1) is a factor.

scheme.pt: Finds a trial root and states the factor

remarks: Long division errors are common — synthetic division (coefficients 1, −4, 1, 6) is faster and safer.
mistakes: Writing the product of roots as d/a instead of −d/a for a cubic.
tips: List the divisors of the constant term before trying roots.

summary: Identity: true for all x. Conditional equation: true for some x only. Degree = highest power.
Linear: ax + b = 0 → x = −b/a. Clear fractions with the LCM first.
Two unknowns: elimination, substitution, cross-multiplication x/(b₁c₂ − b₂c₁) = y/(c₁a₂ − c₂a₁) = 1/(a₁b₂ − a₂b₁).
Unique solution if a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂; none if a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂; infinitely many if all three equal.
Quadratic: x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)]/2a; α + β = −b/a; αβ = c/a; equation x² − Sx + P = 0.
D = b² − 4ac: 0 equal; > 0 square rational unequal; > 0 non-square irrational unequal; < 0 imaginary.
Cubic: find a trial root k, divide by (x − k), solve the quadratic; Σα = −b/a, Σαβ = c/a, αβγ = −d/a.
remember: Reciprocal roots → c = a. Opposite roots → b = 0.
Irrational/imaginary roots come in conjugate pairs.
Reject roots that break the story (negative counts, negative prices, √ negative).
traps: Sum of roots is −b/a, not b/a.
In cross-multiplication keep the equations in "= 0" form with signs.

viva.q: What is the difference between a conditional equation and an identity?
viva.model: A conditional equation is true only for particular values of the variable, which are its roots. An identity is true for every value of the variable, for example x plus one whole squared equals x squared plus two x plus one.

viva.q: When do two linear equations in two unknowns have a unique solution, no solution, or infinitely many solutions?
viva.model: If the ratio of the x coefficients is not equal to the ratio of the y coefficients, the lines intersect and there is a unique solution. If those two ratios are equal but the ratio of the constants is different, the lines are parallel and there is no solution. If all three ratios are equal, the lines coincide and there are infinitely many solutions.

viva.q: How do you solve a cubic equation in the CA Foundation exam?

cases.title: Pricing a new snack pack
cases.case: Raghav Foods is launching a snack pack. Market research suggests that at a price of ₹p per pack it will sell q = 1,200 − 20p packs a week. Weekly costs are a fixed ₹6,000 plus ₹20 per pack. Weekly profit is therefore π = p(1,200 − 20p) − [6,000 + 20(1,200 − 20p)], which simplifies to π = −20p² + 1,600p − 30,000.
